paragraphs.mainIdea: George is bored. He has no brother or sister and no friends near the farm. He is tired of Grandma most of all.
paragraphs.simple: George felt very bored. He had no brother or sister. His father was a farmer. The farm was far from everything, so there were no children to play with. George was tired of looking at pigs, hens, cows and sheep. Most of all, he was tired of living in the same house as his bad-tempered old Grandma. It was not a fun way to spend a Saturday morning, looking after her on his own.

paragraphs.context: she was always complaining, grousing, grouching, grumbling, griping about something or other
paragraphs.mainIdea: Most grandmothers are kind, but George's Grandma is not. She only thinks about herself, and she always complains.
paragraphs.simple: Most grandmothers are kind and nice, but not this one. She sat in her chair by the window all day, every day. She always said that something was wrong. She was never nice to George. She never smiled at him and asked how he was. She never asked him to play a game, or asked how school was. She only cared about herself. She was a very unhappy, bad-tempered old woman.

paragraphs.context: you've got to be very quick, my dear, when you put one of those in your mouth
paragraphs.mainIdea: Grandma says that an earwig is nice to eat. But you must be quick or it will hold your tongue.
paragraphs.simple: Grandma says that a big fat earwig tastes very good. But you must be very quick when you put one in your mouth. An earwig has a pair of sharp nippers at the back of its body. If it holds your tongue with them, it never lets go. So you must bite the earwig first, before it bites you.

paragraphs.context: have magic powers that can twist the creatures of this earth into wondrous shapes
paragraphs.mainIdea: Grandma speaks in a low, strange voice. She says that some people have magic powers over living things.
paragraphs.simple: Grandma leaned forward in her chair. She spoke in a low voice that George had never heard before. She said, 'Some of us have magic powers. We can change the animals of the earth into wonderful shapes.'

paragraphs.context: he had a tremendous urge to do something about her
paragraphs.mainIdea: George hates Grandma and wants to do something big and shocking to her. He is only eight, but he is brave.
paragraphs.simple: George sat down at the table in the kitchen. He was shaking a little. He hated Grandma very much. He hated that horrible old woman who was like a witch. Suddenly he wanted very much to do something about her. He wanted to do something big, something very exciting, a real shock, a sort of explosion. He wanted to blow away the witch smell that hung about her in the next room. George was only eight years old, but he was a brave little boy. He was ready to fight this old woman.

paragraphs.context: George sat there pondering this interesting problem, his eye fell upon the bottle
paragraphs.mainIdea: George sees Grandma's medicine bottle. He thinks the medicine does her no good. A medicine should make a person better.
paragraphs.simple: George sat there and thought about this interesting problem. Then he saw the bottle of Grandma's brown medicine on the sideboard. It looked like bad stuff. Four times a day she took a big spoonful of it, but it did her no good at all. She was just as horrible after it as before. A medicine, George thought, is for making a person better. If it does not do that, it is of no use.

paragraphs.context: I shall make her a new medicine, one that is so strong and so fierce
paragraphs.mainIdea: George decides to make a new medicine for Grandma. It will be so strong that it will cure her or blow her head off.
paragraphs.simple: George thought, 'Now I know what to do! I will make her a new medicine. It will be so strong and so wild that it will either make her well or blow off the top of her head. It will be a magic medicine. No doctor in the world has ever made one like it.'

paragraphs.context: George had absolutely no doubts whatsoever about how he was going to make his famous medicine
paragraphs.mainIdea: George has a clear plan. He will put in everything he can find that is runny, powdery or sticky.
paragraphs.simple: George had no doubts at all about how he was going to make his famous medicine. He was not going to play around and wonder whether to put in a little of this or a little of that. He was going to put in everything he could find. He would not stop to think. The rule was this: whatever he saw that was runny or powdery or sticky, in it went.

paragraphs.context: he gazed longingly at the famous and dreaded medicine cupboard
paragraphs.mainIdea: George must not touch the medicine cupboard. He made a promise to his parents, so he keeps it.
paragraphs.simple: In the bathroom, George looked for a long time at the medicine cupboard. Everyone knew it and feared it. But he did not go near it. It was the only thing in the house he was not allowed to touch. He had made serious promises to his parents, and he would not break them. They had told him that some things in it could kill a person. He wanted to give Grandma a hot mouthful, but he did not want a dead body on his hands.

paragraphs.context: hair-spray and shaving-cream and shoe-polish are all very well and they will no doubt cause some splendid explosions
paragraphs.mainIdea: George thinks that the things he has used will cause some good bangs. But he wants some real medicine to make the mixture stronger.
paragraphs.simple: George said to himself, 'Let us be honest. Hair spray, shaving cream and shoe polish are all very well. They will surely cause some great bangs inside the old man. But the magic mixture now needs a little of the real stuff, real pills and real tonics, to give it punch and muscle.'

paragraphs.context: CAUTION, DO NOT MAKE THE MIXTURE ANY STRONGER OR THE WOOL WILL FALL OUT
paragraphs.mainIdea: A bottle of sheep medicine has a warning on the label. If the mixture is too strong, the sheep will lose its wool.
paragraphs.simple: The next bottle had a bright red liquid in it. The label said it was for sheep with sheeprot, and for getting rid of ticks and fleas. You mixed one spoonful in one gallon of water and poured it over the sheep. The label warned you to be careful. If the mixture was any stronger, the wool would fall out and the animal would be naked.

paragraphs.context: It was a brutal and bewitching smell, spicy and staggering, fierce and frenzied
paragraphs.mainIdea: The mixture makes a strong, wonderful smell and a blue smoke. George feels as if it is alive.
paragraphs.simple: Soon the mixture began to bubble and foam. A rich blue smoke, the colour of a peacock, came up from it. A hot, wild smell filled the kitchen. It made George choke and splutter. He had never smelled a smell like it. It was a rough, magic smell, spicy and strong, fierce and wild, full of wizardry and magic. Each time he smelled it, firecrackers went off in his head and electric prickles ran along the backs of his legs. It was wonderful to stir this amazing mixture and watch it smoke and bubble as if it were alive. Once, he could have sworn he saw bright sparks in the swirling foam.

paragraphs.context: he couldn't help thinking back upon all the mad and marvellous things that had gone into the making
paragraphs.mainIdea: George thinks about all the crazy things he put in the medicine as he pours it into the spoon.
paragraphs.simple: George took out the cork and slowly began to pour the thick brown stuff into the spoon. He could not stop thinking about all the mad and wonderful things he had put into it. There was the shaving soap, the hair remover, the dandruff cure, the washing-machine powder, the flea powder for dogs, the shoe polish, the black pepper and the horseradish sauce. There were also the strong animal pills and powders and liquids. And there was the brown paint.

paragraphs.context: her whole body shot up whoosh into the air
paragraphs.mainIdea: Grandma takes the medicine and shoots up in the air. She stays there, stiff and shaking.
paragraphs.simple: Grandma yelled 'Oweeeee!' and her whole body shot up into the air with a whoosh. It was as if someone had put an electric wire under her chair and switched it on. She went up like a jack-in-the-box. She did not come down. She stayed there in the air, about two feet up, still in a sitting position. But now she could not move. She was shaking, her eyes were bulging and her hair was standing straight up.

paragraphs.context: A sizzling sound, the kind you get if you hold a hot frying-pan under a cold tap
paragraphs.mainIdea: George pours water into Grandma's mouth to put out the fire. Water comes out of her and the smoke goes away.
paragraphs.simple: George ran into the kitchen and came back with a jug of water. 'Open your mouth, Grandma!' he cried. He could hardly see her because of the smoke, but he poured half a jugful down her throat. A sizzling sound, like a hot frying-pan under a cold tap, came from deep in Grandma's stomach. The old woman jumped and snorted. She gasped and made noises in her throat. Water shot out of her, and the smoke went away.

paragraphs.context: this ancient scrawny old woman getting taller and taller, longer and longer, thinner and thinner
paragraphs.mainIdea: Grandma grows taller and thinner, like something being pulled up by hands that no one can see.

paragraphs.context: It jumped high in the air and turned a complete somersault, then landed back on its feet
paragraphs.mainIdea: After the fire goes out, the hen feels better. It jumps high and turns over in the air.
paragraphs.simple: Now that the fire was out, the hen seemed better. It stood up well. It moved its wings up and down. Then it got low to the ground, as if it were getting ready to jump. And it did jump. It jumped high in the air, turned right over, and landed on its feet.

paragraphs.context: Mr Kranky was a small man with bandy legs and a huge head
paragraphs.mainIdea: This tells us about George's father. He is kind, but he gets very excited about small things. He is very excited about the big hen.
paragraphs.simple: Then George's father came. His name was Mr Killy Kranky. He was a small man with bent legs and a big head. He was kind to George, but he was not an easy person to live with. Even the smallest things made him excited. The hen in the yard was not a small thing. When he saw it, he jumped about as if something were burning his feet. 'Great heavens!' he cried, and waved his arms. 'What is this? What has happened? Where did it come from? It is a giant hen! Who did it?'

paragraphs.context: In a way, the medicine had done Grandma good
paragraphs.mainIdea: The medicine has not changed Grandma's bad temper. But it has made her feel well. She rides George's big pony.
paragraphs.simple: In a way, the medicine had done Grandma some good. It had not made her any less grumpy or bad-tempered. But it seemed to have cured all her aches and pains, and she was as frisky as a ferret. As soon as the crane put her down, she ran to George's huge pony, Jack Frost, and jumped on his back. This very old woman, who was now as tall as a house, rode fast around the farm on the giant pony. She jumped over trees and sheds and shouted, 'Out of my way! Clear the decks! Stand back, all you miserable midgets, or I will trample you to death!' She said other silly things like that.

paragraphs.context: we need barrels and barrels of it! Tons and tons!
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mr Kranky wants to make a lot of the medicine. He plans to sell it to farmers all over the world. He thinks he and George will be rich.
paragraphs.simple: Mr Kranky cried, 'My dear boy, we need barrels and barrels of it! Tons and tons! Then we will sell it to every farmer in the world, so they can all have giant animals! We will build a Marvellous Medicine Factory. We will sell the stuff in bottles at five pounds each. We will be rich, and you will be famous!'

paragraphs.context: working himself up so much that he put butter in his coffee and milk on his toast
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mr Kranky is so excited that he makes mistakes at breakfast. He thinks that the medicine will end hunger in the world.
paragraphs.simple: 'There is no time to wait!' cried Mr Kranky. He was so excited that he put butter in his coffee and milk on his toast. 'Do you not understand what your great invention will do for the world? No one will ever be hungry again!'

paragraphs.context: The chicken looked perfectly absurd with its long long legs and its ordinary little body perched high up on top
paragraphs.mainIdea: The second medicine makes the chicken's legs grow very long, but its body does not grow. It looks very strange.
paragraphs.simple: The legs kept growing. The more they grew, the higher the chicken's body went. When the legs were about fifteen feet long, they stopped. The chicken looked very silly with its very long legs and its normal little body high on top. It was like a chicken on tall sticks.

paragraphs.context: I'll be blowed if I'm going to starve as well
paragraphs.mainIdea: Grandma is very angry. She is hungry because no one has brought her any food, and she has to sleep outside.
paragraphs.simple: At that moment, Grandma came walking into the yard with long steps. She looked down from her great height at the three people below her and shouted, 'What is going on around here? Why has no one brought me my morning cup of tea? It is bad enough to sleep in the yard with the rats and mice, but I will not starve as well! No tea! No eggs and bacon! No buttered toast!'

paragraphs.context: Grandma's tiny face still bore the same foul and furious expression it had always had
paragraphs.mainIdea: Grandma is getting smaller, but she is still angry. She asks how anyone would feel.

'How do you think I feel? How would you feel if a minute ago you were a great giant and now you are a horrible little midget?'

paragraphs.context: I suppose it's all for the best, really. She was a bit of a nuisance around the house
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mrs Kranky looks for Grandma and is puzzled. Soon she is calm and says that Grandma was a bit of a nuisance.
paragraphs.simple: For a few minutes, Mrs Kranky walked around with a puzzled look on her face. She said, 'Mother, where are you? Where have you gone? How can I find you?' But she soon calmed down. By lunchtime she was saying, 'Well, I suppose it is all for the best, really. She was a bit of a nuisance around the house, was she not?'

paragraphs.context: he had touched with the very tips of his fingers the edge of a magic world
paragraphs.mainIdea: George says nothing. He feels shaky. He knows that something very big has happened.
paragraphs.simple: George did not say a word. He felt shaky. He knew that something very big had happened that morning. For a few short moments, he had touched the edge of a magic world with the ends of his fingers.

sentences.context: Boys who grow too fast become stupid and lazy
sentences.simple: Boys who grow up too fast become stupid and lazy, Grandma says.
sentences.grammar: 'Who grow too fast' tells us which boys; 'too fast' means faster than is good; 'become' shows a change.

sentences.context: I gave up growing when I was extremely small
sentences.simple: I stopped growing when I was very, very small.
sentences.grammar: After 'gave up' we use the -ing form (growing); 'gave up growing' means stopped growing.

sentences.context: That's old enough to know better
sentences.simple: You are eight, Grandma says. You are old enough to know how to act.
sentences.grammar: 'Adjective + enough to + verb' means has enough of it to do something; 'know better' means know the right way to act.

sentences.context: George couldn't help disliking Grandma
sentences.simple: George could not stop himself. He did not like Grandma.
sentences.grammar: 'Can't help + -ing' means cannot stop yourself from doing it.

sentences.context: Never once, even on her best days, had she smiled at George
sentences.simple: Even on her best days, she had not smiled at George, not even one time.
sentences.grammar: 'Never once' at the start of a sentence puts 'had' before 'she' (had she smiled); this makes the sentence strong.

sentences.context: if it grabs your tongue with those, it never lets go
sentences.simple: If an earwig holds your tongue with its sharp nippers, it never lets go.
sentences.grammar: 'If + present, present' tells what is always true; 'those' means the earwig's sharp nippers.

sentences.context: so much the better
sentences.simple: If there are caterpillars in the cabbage, that is even better.
sentences.grammar: 'So much the better' is a fixed saying that means even better; 'it's got' means 'it has got'.

sentences.context: Could it be, George wondered, that she was a witch?
sentences.simple: George asked himself if Grandma might be a witch.
sentences.grammar: 'Could it be that...?' asks if something may be true; 'George wondered' is put in the middle of the question.

sentences.context: We know how to have you wake up in the morning with a long tail
sentences.simple: We know how to make you wake up in the morning with a long tail coming out behind you.
sentences.grammar: 'Have you wake up' means make you wake up; 'have + person + verb' means make something happen to that person.

sentences.context: He may have been only eight years old but he was a brave little boy
sentences.simple: George was only eight, but he was brave.
sentences.grammar: 'May have been ... but' means it is true that he was only eight, but he was brave anyway.

sentences.context: The whole point of medicine, surely, was to make a person better
sentences.simple: Medicine is for making a person well. If it does not do that, it is no use.
sentences.grammar: 'The point of X was to + verb' tells what X is for; the sentence has 'surely' in the middle.

sentences.context: it will either cure her completely or blow off the top of her head
sentences.simple: It will make her completely well, or it will blow off the top of her head.
sentences.grammar: 'Either ... or ...' shows two choices.

sentences.context: He would have liked to put a firework banger under her chair but he didn't have one
sentences.simple: George wished he could put a loud firework under her chair, but he did not have one.
sentences.grammar: 'Would have liked to + verb' tells about a wish for something that did not happen.

sentences.context: Quite simply, he was going to put in EVERYTHING he could find
sentences.simple: He would just put in everything that he found.
sentences.grammar: 'Was going to' tells a plan; 'he could find' tells which things.

sentences.context: whatever he saw, if it was runny or powdery or gooey, in it went
sentences.simple: Anything he saw that was runny, powdery or sticky went into the pan.
sentences.grammar: 'Whatever' means anything that; 'in it went' puts 'in' first and means 'it went in'.

sentences.context: he was out to give Grandma a pretty fiery mouthful
sentences.simple: George wanted to give Grandma a very hot mouthful, like fire.
sentences.grammar: 'Be out to + verb' means be trying to do something.

sentences.context: George didn't know whether Grandma was automatic or not
sentences.simple: George did not know if Grandma was 'automatic', like the washing-machines, or not.
sentences.grammar: 'Whether ... or not' means 'if it is true or not'; we use it after 'know'.

sentences.context: what the magic mixture now needs is a touch of the real stuff
sentences.simple: The magic mixture now needs a little real medicine.
sentences.grammar: 'What + subject + verb' (what the mixture needs) is the subject of 'is'; this puts the main point at the end.

sentences.context: Nobody had ever told him he mustn't touch them
sentences.simple: No one had ever said that he must not touch them.
sentences.grammar: 'Had told' (past perfect) is an earlier time in the past; 'mustn't' means it is not allowed.

sentences.context: MORE THAN THAT WILL MAKE THE PIG ROCK AND ROLL
sentences.simple: If you give more than that, the pig will 'rock and roll'. This is a joke on the label.
sentences.grammar: 'More than that' is the subject (a bigger amount); 'make the pig + verb' means cause the pig to do it.

sentences.context: It simply must be brown or she'll get suspicious
sentences.simple: It has to be brown, or she will think something is wrong.
sentences.grammar: 'Must ... or ...' means: this must happen, or something bad will happen; 'she'll' means 'she will'.

sentences.context: Don't interrupt me in the middle of a sentence!
sentences.simple: Do not stop me while I am still speaking!
sentences.grammar: 'Don't + verb' is a command not to do something; 'in the middle of' means before it is finished.

sentences.context: You'd have thought she'd swallowed a red-hot poker the way she took off from that chair
sentences.simple: She went off the chair so fast, you would think she had swallowed a red-hot metal stick.
sentences.grammar: 'You'd have thought she'd swallowed' means 'you would have thought she had swallowed'; it says how it looked, but it was not true.

sentences.context: I'll be fried to a frizzle! I'll be boiled like a beetroot!
sentences.simple: Grandma cries that she will be cooked until she is burnt, and boiled like a beetroot.
sentences.grammar: 'I'll be + fried/boiled' is passive: it tells what will be done to her; the words are a joke.

sentences.context: She was going down. She was slowly getting thinner again
sentences.simple: She was coming down. Slowly she was getting thinner again.
sentences.grammar: 'Getting + thinner' shows a change that is happening now; 'again' means as she was before.

sentences.context: As George removed the cork and began very slowly to pour the thick brown stuff
sentences.simple: George took out the cork and began to pour the thick brown stuff very slowly.
sentences.grammar: 'As' means at the same time; 'very slowly' sits between 'began' and 'to pour'.

sentences.context: Hens don't do any laying after they've been on fire!
sentences.simple: Grandma says that hens do not lay eggs after they have been on fire.
sentences.grammar: 'Don't do any laying' is another way to say 'don't lay'; 'they've been' is 'they have been'.

sentences.context: Compared with me, that hen is titchy small!
sentences.simple: Grandma says that the hen is very, very small next to her.
sentences.grammar: 'Compared with + noun' at the start means 'if you put the two side by side'; 'titchy' means very small.

sentences.context: He had never seen anything like it. But then who had?
sentences.simple: He had never seen anything like it, and no one else had either.
sentences.grammar: 'Who had?' is a short question for 'who had seen anything like it?'; it means no one had.

sentences.context: even the smallest things got him all worked up and excited
sentences.simple: Even very small things made him very excited.
sentences.grammar: 'Got him all worked up' means made him very excited; 'even' stresses that the things were small.

sentences.context: we'll test it out on an old hen just to make absolutely sure
sentences.simple: We will try it on an old hen to be very sure.
sentences.grammar: 'Just to + verb' gives the reason; 'test it out' means try it.

sentences.context: If anything is empty, it means you used it.
sentences.simple: An empty bottle or can shows that you used it.
sentences.grammar: 'If + present, present' tells what is always true; 'anything' is used in an 'if' sentence.

sentences.context: Because if we've forgotten even one tiny thing, then it won't work!
sentences.simple: If we have forgotten even one small thing, it will not work!
sentences.grammar: 'If + have forgotten' talks about something that may have happened; 'won't' is 'will not' and gives the result.

sentences.context: I must have left something out
sentences.simple: I am sure that I did not put in one thing.
sentences.grammar: 'Must have + left' is a strong guess about the past; 'leave out' means not put in.

sentences.context: There's probably just one vital thing missing
sentences.simple: Maybe one very important thing is not in the mixture.
sentences.grammar: 'There's' means 'there is'; 'missing' after 'thing' means that is not there.

sentences.context: I'll be blowed if I'm going to starve as well!
sentences.simple: I will not go hungry on top of all that!
sentences.grammar: 'I'll be blowed if...' is an old, strong way to say 'I will not'; 'as well' means also.

get up to.meaning: To do something, often something bad.

be up to.meaning: To be doing something that others do not know about.

keep out of.meaning: To stay away from a place or thing.

get away.meaning: To escape from a person or place.
get away.example: trying to get away from me

take on.meaning: To get ready to fight or face someone.
take on.example: He was ready to take this old woman on.

shake up.meaning: To give someone a big surprise or a fright.
shake up.example: shake the old woman up a bit

blow off.meaning: To make something fly off with a bang.
blow off.example: blow off the top of her head

fool about.meaning: To play or waste time and not be serious.

mess about.meaning: To play or waste time and not be serious.

smell a rat.meaning: To feel that something is wrong.

let off steam.meaning: To let out strong feeling, or to let steam out.
forms: let off a bit of steam
let off steam.example: she’s let off a bit of steam

cook one's goose.meaning: To spoil someone's plans or chances.
cook one's goose.example: You’ve cooked the old girl’s goose!

fed up.meaning: Tired of something and unhappy about it.
fed up.example: George looked pretty fed up, too.

calm down.meaning: To become less angry or less excited.

turn up.meaning: To make a light, sound or heat bigger.

turn off.meaning: To stop a machine or heat.

cool down.example: time for it to cool down

boil up.meaning: To heat something until it boils.
boil up.example: I shall have to boil it all up,

stir up.meaning: To mix things together by moving them round.

steady on.meaning: A way to tell someone to slow down.

work up.meaning: To make someone more and more excited or angry.

get cracking.example: We must get cracking at once.

keep at it.meaning: To go on trying and not stop.

dish out.meaning: To give something out to someone.

leave out.example: I know you left something out!

write down.example: I’ll write down each and every item.

wait and see.meaning: To wait to find out what will happen.

hold one's nose.meaning: To close your nose with your fingers so you cannot smell.

go off.example: firecrackers went off in his skull

by golly.example: By golly, you really are on fire,

all of a sudden.meaning: Very quickly, with no time to get ready.
all of a sudden.example: all of a sudden he had a tremendous urge

on purpose.meaning: Because you want to, not by chance.

look after.example: Looking after her all by himself

come on.meaning: A way to tell someone to hurry or to try.

for once.meaning: This one time, but not often.
